summary: SMIv2 is the language for MIB modules used with SNMP, and YANG is the data modeling language used with NETCONF. This RFC defines how to translate SMIv2 MIB modules into YANG modules.

eli5.summary: Two groups write their rules in different languages. This is a guide for translating the old one into the new one.

questions: how to convert a mib to yang
how does smiv2 map to yang
why are translated mib objects read only
how are snmp tables mapped to yang lists
subtitle: The rulebook for turning SNMP MIB modules into read-only YANG modules that NETCONF can serve.

tldr.problem: Network devices already describe their management data in SMIv2 MIB modules for SNMP, but NETCONF uses YANG. Without a standard translation, every tool would convert MIB modules differently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives translation rules for each SMIv2 construct (modules, imports, textual conventions, objects, tables, notifications). It adds a small YANG module of extensions, ietf-yang-smiv2, to keep SMIv2 details that YANG has no place for.
tldr.outcome: SMIv2 objects become read-only (config false) YANG nodes reachable via NETCONF. Making any of them writable is a separate, deliberate step done with YANG deviations.

today: RFC 6643 is a Proposed Standard, published in July 2012, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It relies on YANG as defined in RFC 6020 and NETCONF as defined in RFC 6241.

sections.title: Why Translate MIB Modules
sections.content:
SMIv2 is the language used to write MIB modules for SNMP. YANG is the data modeling language used with NETCONF. RFC 6643 describes how to translate SMIv2 modules into YANG modules so that SMIv2 objects can be read through NETCONF.

The result is always read-only: the generated nodes are config false, even when the SMIv2 object was read-write or read-create. Section 11 of the RFC explains why.

Generated YANG modules should not be edited by hand. If a change is needed, the RFC says to change the original SMIv2 module (updating its LAST-UPDATED and REVISION clauses) and run the translation again. YANG augments and deviations can still be applied to the generated module like any other. SMIv1 modules are handled in two steps: first convert to SMIv2 using RFC 3584, then apply this RFC.
sections.eli5: Imagine a recipe written in one language that you want to cook from in another. This RFC is the dictionary that says how to translate every word, and it says do not scribble on the translation, fix the original instead.

sections.title: Types, Modules and Imports
sections.content:
An SMIv2 module becomes a YANG module with the same name. Its namespace is the IANA-registered prefix urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:smiv2: followed by the SMIv2 module name. The YANG prefix MAY be derived from the module name with the algorithm in Appendix B, which joins lowercase name tokens until the prefix is unique.

Base types map by Appendix A. For example Integer32 becomes int32, Unsigned32 becomes uint32, Counter32 becomes counter32 and TruthValue becomes boolean. An OCTET STRING becomes a YANG string if it has a DISPLAY-HINT and binary if it does not. An INTEGER becomes an enumeration or an int32 depending on use.

SMIv2 IMPORT clauses import named symbols, while a YANG import pulls in a whole module. So the RFC gives a step-by-step procedure that skips SNMPv2-SMI and SNMPv2-CONF, skips textual conventions already covered by Appendix A, and only generates imports for items used in SYNTAX, OBJECTS, INDEX or AUGMENTS clauses. Every module also imports ietf-yang-smiv2 with the prefix smiv2.
sections.eli5: Each kind of box in the old system has a matching box in the new one. A shopping list of what you need to fetch is made from only the things you actually use, not everything in the shop.

sections.title: Modules, Conventions and Identities
sections.content:
The MODULE-IDENTITY macro supplies a module's contact and history. Its ORGANIZATION, CONTACT-INFO and DESCRIPTION clauses become the YANG organization, contact and description statements. Each REVISION clause becomes a YANG revision. A LAST-UPDATED date that matches no revision gets an extra revision statement. A top-level container named after the module is generated, and it MUST be config false.

A TEXTUAL-CONVENTION becomes a YANG typedef with the same name. SYNTAX maps to type, range limits to range, length limits to length, enumerations to enum/value and BITS to bit/position. STATUS maps to status unless it is current. The DISPLAY-HINT is kept as an smiv2:display-hint statement.

An OBJECT-IDENTITY becomes a YANG identity whose base is smiv2:object-identity, and a plain OBJECT IDENTIFIER assignment becomes an smiv2:alias statement.
sections.eli5: The title page, the list of changes and the name tags of the old document all get copied to the matching places in the new one. Anything that is normal and expected, like a status of current, is simply left unwritten.

sections.title: Objects, Tables and Notifications
sections.content:
Scalar and columnar OBJECT-TYPE objects become YANG leaf statements. A scalar's leaf sits in a container named after its parent node in the OID tree. If that parent has several names, the automatic translation MUST fail with an error and a human has to resolve the clash. Each leaf keeps its SMIv2 MAX-ACCESS, DEFVAL and object identifier as smiv2:max-access, smiv2:defval and smiv2:oid.

A conceptual table becomes a container, and its row becomes a list inside it. The SMIv2 INDEX clause becomes the list's key. If the same object appears twice in INDEX, a suffix such as _2 is added to the repeat. Index objects that live in another table become leafref leaves. An IMPLIED index is recorded with smiv2:implied.

A table or row that augments another table becomes an smiv2:alias plus a YANG augment pointing at the augmented table. A NOTIFICATION-TYPE becomes a YANG notification. Each object in its OBJECTS clause becomes a container named object-1, object-2 and so on, holding leafrefs to the index objects and to the object itself.
sections.eli5: A spreadsheet in the old language becomes a spreadsheet in the new one: each table keeps its rows, the key column stays the key, and alarm messages list exactly which cells they are about.

sections.title: The ietf-yang-smiv2 Extension Module
sections.content:
Some SMIv2 information has no home in core YANG. Section 10 defines the YANG module ietf-yang-smiv2 (prefix smiv2) with extension statements to carry it:

  • smiv2:display-hint, smiv2:max-access and smiv2:defval preserve those SMIv2 clauses.
  • smiv2:implied records an IMPLIED index object.
  • smiv2:alias, smiv2:oid and smiv2:subid carry descriptors and numeric object identifiers.

The module also defines the identity object-identity and a typedef opaque for the SMIv2 Opaque type. It notes that the MAX-ACCESS value has no impact on the access NETCONF gives to YANG objects.
sections.eli5: Some labels from the old language do not fit anywhere in the new one. So the new document gets a few sticky notes to carry that extra information along.

sections.title: Read-Only Results and Config Deviations
sections.content:
All translated nodes are config false. The RFC gives two reasons. First, SNMP and NETCONF handle persistence differently: with SNMP it depends on the object's definition or on a StorageType column, with NETCONF it depends on the datastore. Second, NETCONF as defined in RFC 6241 has no standard operation to modify operational state, because <edit-config> and <copy-config> only manipulate configuration data. So configuration nodes cannot be generated automatically.

Where SNMP and NETCONF persistence semantics agree, an implementation may choose to make some nodes configurable. It should document that in a separate YANG module using deviate replace to change config from false to true. Such a deviation does not affect compliance with the generated module. Deviations apply to the target node only and are not inherited by children, so each node must be listed. The RFC's example does this for the RMON2-MIB addressMapControlTable and advertises the deviation module in the NETCONF hello capabilities.
sections.eli5: By default you may look at everything but not change anything. If someone wants to allow changes to some things, they write a short extra note that says exactly which ones.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC says the translation itself has no security impact on the Internet. Users of YANG models generated from published SMIv2 RFCs should read the security considerations of those RFCs, which explain which objects are sensitive. NETCONF users are encouraged to use the access control model in RFC 6536.

IANA registered two URIs in the IETF XML registry, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-yang-smiv2 and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:smiv2. It also registered the YANG module ietf-yang-smiv2 with the prefix smiv2.
sections.eli5: Translating the document does not open any new doors. If some information is private, keep using the same locks the original document recommended.

items.title: display-hint
items.text: Carries the DISPLAY-HINT of a textual convention.

items.title: max-access
items.text: Carries MAX-ACCESS; it does not change NETCONF access.

items.title: defval
items.text: Carries the DEFVAL default in the SMIv2 value space.

items.title: implied
items.text: Names an INDEX object preceded by IMPLIED.

items.title: alias
items.text: Introduces an SMIv2 descriptor, with an oid inside.

items.title: oid and subid
items.text: Give the numeric object identifier or its last sub-identifier.
